obj.quote: The Statistical Requirements Compendium (SRC), published by Eurostat, serves as a reference document for the EU acquis in statistics. This handbook has been prepared as a practical tool at the disposal of compilers of ESA 2010-based national and regional accounts. Its objective is to translate the voluntary EU recommendations on data revisions into specific practices ensuring accurate, reliable, consistent and comparable data. The handbook provides good practices for routine and benchmark revisions as well as for non-scheduled revisions.

Routine revisions (or current revisions) are changes in published data which are related to the regular data production process and encompass all changes in national accounts estimates for a particular period from the first to the final estimate. … Benchmark revisions … Revisions of data sources or methods … covering large time series … resolving classification issues, implementing major changes …

Benchmark revisions should take place for reference years ending with ‘0’ and ‘5’, with implementation years ending with ‘4’ and ‘9’. … Routine revisions … depth limits … Quarterly – 15 quarters (Q1), 16 (Q2), unlimited (Q3), 18 (Q4) …
obj.notes: Destatis already cited the 2024 major revision and 2029 next; this supplies the EU-level rule that governs those pulses.

obj.quote: Revisions must align with the ESA 2010 TP (Annex B to Regulation (EU) No 549/2013); revised data transmitted no later than publication day … Assessed via ESA 2010 quality reporting (Regulation (EU) No 549/2013, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/2304).

The depth of the quarterly routine revisions is limited to a maximum of: 15 quarters in the 1st quarter; 16 quarters in the 2nd quarter; unlimited in the 3rd quarter; 18 quarters in the 4th quarter. The depth of the annual routine revisions is limited to a maximum of: 3 years in the 1st quarter …; 1 year in the 2nd quarter …; unlimited in the 3rd quarter; 1 year in the 4th quarter …

A benchmark revision should be publicly announced in advance of the release date (at least a quarter in advance for annual and quarterly statistics). … Metadata should contain adequate information on: the reasons for the revision … the scope of the revisions … revision size … inconsistencies with related and not (yet) revised statistics … possible breaks in timeseries …

obj.quote: Statistics on the balance sheets of monetary financial institutions (MFIs) were first published by the ECB in December 1998. These statistics cover euro area credit institutions, other financial institutions carrying out “bank-like” business and money market funds. They form the main input for compilation of euro area monetary aggregates.
names: Manual on MFI balance sheet statistics (February 2024)

obj.location: 7 Compilation of euro area statistics / introductory paragraph
obj.quote: The main source of information for euro area monetary statistics (monetary aggregates and counterparts of M3) is the MFI balance sheet, aggregated across the euro area and then consolidated (inter-MFI positions cancelled out).
names: euro area monetary statistics (monetary aggregates and counterparts of M3)

obj.location: 7.1.2 The euro area consolidated MFI balance sheet
obj.quote: The starting point for derivation of the consolidated balance sheet is the aggregated balance sheet of the MFI sector as a whole. The consolidated balance sheet of the euro area MFI sector provides statistical information on the sector’s assets and liabilities vis-à-vis residents of the euro area outside the MFI sector (i.e. general government and all other euro area residents) and vis-à-vis non-residents of the euro area; it is obtained by netting the inter-MFI positions within the euro area.
names: euro area consolidated MFI balance sheet

obj.quote: A monetary aggregate can be defined as the sum of currency in circulation plus the outstanding amounts of certain financial instruments that have a high degree of moneyness, or liquidity in a broad sense. The Eurosystem has defined a narrow (M1), an intermediate (M2) and a broad aggregate (M3). These aggregates differ with respect to the degree of moneyness of the financial instruments included. The table below shows the definitions of the euro area monetary aggregates comprising liabilities issued by the MFI sector and by entities in the central government sector and certain POGIs in the euro area. These aggregates include only positions of the euro area money-holding sector held with MFIs resident in the euro area.

obj.notes: Table defines the exact instrument composition of each aggregate.

obj.quote: M1 (narrow money) comprises currency in circulation (banknotes and coins) and balances that can immediately be converted into currency or used for cashless payments (overnight deposits).

M2 (intermediate money) comprises M1 plus deposits with original maturities of up to two years and deposits redeemable at notice of up to three months. Depending on their degree of moneyness, such deposits can be converted into components of narrow money; in some cases, however, there may be restrictions, such as the need for advance notification, delays, penalties or fees. The definition of M2 reflects the particular interest in analysing and monitoring a monetary aggregate that includes a wide range of other deposits in addition to currency and overnight deposits.
names: deposits with original maturities of up to two years
deposits redeemable at notice of up to three months

obj.quote: M3 (broad money) comprises M2 plus marketable instruments issued by the MFI sector. Certain money market instruments, in particular MMF shares/units and repurchase agreements, are included in this aggregate. M3 also includes bonds issued by MFIs with an original maturity of up to two years. A high degree of liquidity and price certainty make these instruments close substitutes for deposits. Their inclusion means that M3 is less affected by substitution between various liquid asset categories than narrower definitions of money and is therefore more stable.
names: bonds issued by MFIs with an original maturity of up to two years

obj.quote: 1. The tools used by the Eurosystem in the implementation of monetary policy shall consist of: (a) open market operations; (b) standing facilities; (c) minimum reserve requirements. 2. The minimum reserve requirements are specified in Regulation (EC) No 2531/98 and Regulation (EU) 2021/378 (ECB/2021/1). obj.location: Overview of open market operations / Article on categories
obj.quote: The Eurosystem may conduct open market operations to steer interest rates, manage the liquidity situation in the financial market and signal the stance of monetary policy. Depending on their specific purpose, open market operations can be grouped under the following categories: (a) main refinancing operations; (b) longer-term refinancing operations; (c) fine-tuning operations; (d) structural operations. Open market operations shall be conducted by means of the following instruments: (a) reverse transactions; (b) foreign exchange swaps for monetary policy purposes; (c) the collection of fixed-term deposits; (d) the issuance of ECB debt certificates; (e) outright transactions.
names: foreign exchange swaps for monetary policy purposes

obj.location: Open market operations / What open market operations do
obj.quote: Open market operations (OMO) are our main tools for steering interest rates and managing liquidity in the euro area banking system. They also ensure that our monetary policy stance is transmitted smoothly to the economy. Open market operations allow the Eurosystem to influence the conditions at which banks borrow and lend money. They support three main aims: Signal the monetary policy stance through our key interest rates; Manage liquidity, ensuring that the banking system has enough funds to operate in an orderly way; Steer short term interest rates so that they remain aligned with the policy stance set by the Governing Council.

Main refinancing operations (MROs) Our regular reverse transactions that provide liquidity, usually with a frequency and duration of one week. They are executed in a decentralised manner by the national central banks on the basis of standard tender procedures and according to an indicative calendar.

Three-month longer term refinancing operations (LTROs) Reverse transactions that provide liquidity for a longer duration than MROs. Regular LTROs have a maturity of three months and are conducted monthly by the Eurosystem on the basis of standard tender procedures in accordance with the indicative calendar.

obj.location: Article 1 Valuation haircuts applied to eligible marketable assets
obj.quote: 1. In accordance with Title VI of Part Four of Guideline (EU) 2015/510 (ECB/2014/60), marketable assets shall be subject to valuation haircuts, as defined in Article 2(97) of Guideline (EU) 2015/510 (ECB/2014/60), at the levels set forth in Table 2 in the Annex to this Guideline. 2. obj.location: Article 2 Determination of haircut categories for marketable assets
obj.quote: Eligible marketable assets shall be allocated to one of the five haircut categories, based on the type of issuer and/or the type of asset, as reflected in Table 1 in the Annex to this Guideline: (a) debt instruments issued by central governments, ECB debt certificates and debt certificates issued by NCBs prior to the date of adoption of the euro in their respective Member State whose currency is the euro are included in haircut category I; (b) debt instruments issued by local and regional government, entities classified as agencies by the Eurosystem, multilateral development banks and international organisations, as well as jumbo covered bonds, are included in haircut category II; (c) traditional covered bonds, other covered bonds and debt instruments issued by non-financial corporations are included in haircut category III; (d) unsecured debt instruments issued by credit institutions and by financial corporations other than credit institutions are included in haircut category IV; (e) asset-backed securities are included in haircut category V, regardless of the classification of the issuer.

obj.quote: The year 2027 marks the end of the current multiannual financial framework (MFF), and the constraints associated with this framework apply in full. obj.location: All expenditure chapter tables, MFF column (cross-cutting)
obj.notes: DISC-07-03, FOURTH SECTION CONFIRMED. Complete inventory of MFF codes appearing in SEC04: 22 distinct codes, every one of the form 7.2.4xx, plus a single exception (7.1.24, item 1 6 5 6, treated at S04-138). SEC04 is Section IV. The digit immediately following '7.2.' is 4 throughout. Sections now agreeing: SEC04 to 4, SEC06 to 6, SEC07 to 7, SEC09 to 9, SEC10 to X. Still an inference — no document in the corpus states the rule — but it now holds for four sections without a genuine counter-example. Two additional observations that sharpen the test: (1) MFF codes are not chapter- or Title-scoped — 7.2.431 appears in Chapters 1 2 and 1 6; 7.2.461 in Chapters 1 6 and 2 5; 7.2.483 in Chapters 1 6, 2 3 and 3 7 — so the code encodes a cost category crossing the nomenclature, with the section digit prefixed. (2) 7.2.49SPEC is alphanumeric; if the equivalent codes in SEC06/07/09/10 are 7.2.69SPEC, 7.2.79SPEC etc., the shared 'SPEC' suffix would make coincidence a much weaker explanation than it currently is. Recommend checking that one code first in any section already held.

obj.location: Item 1 6 5 6 - European Schools, MFF column (cross-section check against SEC06)
obj.notes: PRIORITY — this bears directly on G.16 finding 5 and appears to overturn its hypothesis. G.16 recorded SEC06's European Schools line as carrying MFF code 7.1.26 rather than 7.2.6xx, and hypothesised 'a code shared across all institutions for this specific line rather than a genuine counter-example'. SEC04's European Schools line carries 7.1.24, NOT 7.1.26. The codes are therefore not shared across institutions, and the shared-code hypothesis fails on this evidence. Two readings are available and SEC04 alone cannot separate them: (a) the code family is 7.1.2<section>, i.e. the section digit moves to the final position in the 7.1 heading while sitting in the first position of the third group in the 7.2 heading — which would make this a confirmation of section-encoding rather than an exception to it, and predicts 7.1.27 for SEC07, 7.1.29 for SEC09 and 7.1.2X for SEC10; or (b) the final digit encodes something unrelated to section number and the 4/6 match is coincidence at n=2. Reading (a) is testable against any already-held section — one line, one lookup. SEPARATE FLAG: G.16 records SEC06's European Schools line as item '1 6 4 0', while SEC04 carries it at item 1 6 5 6. Either the sections genuinely number this contribution differently, or the item number in G.16 is a transcription slip. Worth confirming against SEC06_batch.md before either is relied on.

obj.location: Cross-cutting: 1.4 table, 2.2.1 table, Annex I, EXPENDITURE nomenclature table
obj.notes: PRIORITY — fifth instance of the unreconciled-total family, and the first one that the corpus itself explains. Facts: SEC04's narrative sections state Title 1 = 462 534 000 and Budget Total = 555 493 000; the EXPENDITURE nomenclature states Title 1 = 462 171 777 and Total = 555 130 777. Both gaps are exactly 362 223. The entire gap is traceable to item 1 4 0 0 (Other staff), where Annex I gives 13 977 000 and the nomenclature gives 13 614 777 for 2027; the 2026 column agrees on both sides, and each figure set is internally self-consistent (the Annex percentage of 3,07% is computed on the Annex figure, and the nomenclature subtotals reconcile to the nomenclature figure). So this is not a transcription slip in one cell — it is two complete, separately-computed figure sets sitting in one document. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SEC04: the unnumbered preamble at the head of the section (S04-002) states that the Commission has 'exceptionally adjusted the estimates of all Institutions' and that 'It is thus possible that figures referred to in the introduction of a specific budget section are different from those integrated into the Draft Budget.' That is a documented, in-corpus explanation for exactly this shape of divergence: introduction figures are the Institution's own estimate, nomenclature figures are the Commission-adjusted ones. If that same preamble appears in SEC02, SEC09 and SEC10 — it is boilerplate and almost certainly does — then DISC-09-01, DISC-10-01, the SEC02 gap and this one may all be instances of one documented mechanism rather than four unexplained discrepancies. STRONG RECOMMENDATION: before writing the pattern up as a cross-section finding, check (i) whether the same preamble appears in each affected section, and (ii) whether each gap is narrative-versus-nomenclature (explained by the preamble) or headline-versus-own-sum within a single table (NOT explained by it — G.16 finding 4 describes SEC06's gap as the latter, headline total versus its own Title 1+2+10 sum, which the preamble would not account for). Those are two different phenomena and the four-for-four count may be conflating them.
